chapter_approach.heading: How this chapter is taught
chapter_approach.intro: The chapter follows the book's own order: lines that meet, lines that never meet, a line across two lines, drawing parallel lines, and the angle rules that follow. Every rule is reached by reasoning from one earlier fact, so an angle fact is never a thing to memorise.

points.title: Try first, name later
points.text: The hook video leaves two folded-paper lines open: do they meet if they are drawn longer? The words intersect, perpendicular and parallel arrive only after the student has looked at lines.

points.title: Reasoning and measuring are told apart
points.text: Every angle fact is first met by measuring, then justified from a straight angle being 180 degrees. A measured pair may be a degree or two off, and the plan says why.

points.title: One chain of reasons
points.text: Linear pairs prove vertically opposite angles; corresponding angles decide parallel lines; corresponding plus vertically opposite give alternate angles; corresponding plus a linear pair give interior angles on the same side.

points.title: Concept, then practice, topic by topic
points.text: Each idea gets its own topic with one video per concept and a practice concept at the end; interactive tools appear only where handling the angles is the idea. The book's questions follow in their own topic, one question and one video per concept.

modules.module_summary: A square of folded paper shows lines that meet and lines that do not. Two lines that cross make four angles: linear pairs add to a straight angle and vertically opposite angles are equal, proved by reasoning. Measuring and reasoning are told apart, and lines that cross at a right angle are perpendicular.

concepts.concept_name: Creases on a folded paper

content.text:
Across the Line
Use a piece of square paper and fold it in different ways. Now, on the creases formed by the folds, draw lines using a pencil and a scale.
You will notice different lines on the paper. Pick any pair of lines and observe their relationship with each other. Do they meet? If they do not meet within the paper, do you think they would meet if they were extended beyond the paper?

concepts.concept_name: Two lines that meet, and the four angles they make

content.text:
Let us observe a pair of lines that meet each other. You will notice that they meet at a point. When a pair of lines meet each other at a point on a plane surface, we say that the lines intersect each other.
Let us observe what happens when two lines intersect. How many angles do they form? Where line l intersects line m, we can see that four angles are formed: a, b, c and d.
Can two straight lines intersect at more than one point?
Activity 1: Draw two lines on a plain sheet of paper so that they intersect. Measure the four angles formed with a protractor. Draw four such pairs of intersecting lines and measure the angles formed at the points of intersection.
What patterns do you observe among these angles?

content.text:
1. Predict first: if two straight lines cross, how many angles appear, and can they cross twice?
2. Two straight lines can meet at one point only, so four angles are made, a, b, c and d, going round the point.
3. Look at the measured angles in pairs: the ones that are neighbours and the ones that face each other.
4. In every pair of lines drawn, neighbouring angles add to 180 degrees and facing angles are equal, or nearly equal when the pencil is thick.

content.text:
Worked example: Farhan draws two lines that cross and measures the four angles with a protractor, going round the point: a = 63°, b = 117°, c = 63° and d = 117°. What pattern do the four angles show?
1. Neighbouring angles: 63 + 117 = 180, and 117 + 63 = 180.
2. Angles that face each other: a and c are both 63°, and b and d are both 117°.
3. So neighbouring angles add to 180° and facing angles are equal, in this pair of lines.
4. Two straight lines meet at one point only, so there are exactly four angles at the crossing.
Answer: Neighbours add to 180° and facing angles are equal; two straight lines meet at one point only

concepts.concept_name: Linear pairs and the straight angle

content.text:
If ∠a is 120°, can you figure out the measurements of ∠b, ∠c and ∠d, without drawing and measuring them?
We know that ∠a and ∠b together measure 180°, because when they are combined, they form a straight angle which measures 180°. So, if ∠a is 120°, then ∠b must be 60°.
Similarly, ∠b and ∠c together measure 180°. So, if ∠b is 60°, then ∠c must be 120°. And ∠c and ∠d together measure 180°. So, if ∠c is 120°, then ∠d must be 60°.
Therefore, ∠a and ∠c measure 120°, and ∠b and ∠d measure 60°.
Adjacent angles, like ∠a and ∠b, formed by two lines intersecting each other, are called linear pairs. Linear pairs always add up to 180°.

3. Go round the point one angle at a time: each step takes the last angle away from 180°.

content.text:
Worked example: Two lines cross. The angle a is 120°. Find b, c and d going round the point, without measuring.
1. a and b form a linear pair, so b = 180 − 120 = 60.
2. b and c form a linear pair, so c = 180 − 60 = 120.
3. c and d form a linear pair, so d = 180 − 120 = 60.
4. So a and c are 120°, and b and d are 60°.
Answer: b = 60°, c = 120°, d = 60°

concepts.concept_name: Vertically opposite angles, and a proof

content.text:
When two lines intersect each other and form four angles, labelled a, b, c and d, then ∠a and ∠c are equal, and ∠b and ∠d are equal! Is this always true for any pair of intersecting lines?
Check this for different measures of ∠a. Using these measurements, can you reason whether this property holds true for any measure of ∠a?
We can generalise our reasoning without assuming the values of ∠a. Since straight angles measure 180°, we must have ∠a + ∠b = ∠a + ∠d = 180°. Hence, ∠b and ∠d are always equal. Similarly, ∠b + ∠a = ∠b + ∠c = 180°, so ∠a and ∠c must be equal.
Opposite angles, like ∠b and ∠d, formed by two lines intersecting each other, are called vertically opposite angles. Vertically opposite angles are always equal to each other.
From the above reasoning, we conclude that whenever two lines intersect, vertically opposite angles are equal. Such a justification is called a proof in mathematics.

content.text:
Worked example: Two lines cross and a = 35°. Use linear pairs to find b and d, then show that they are equal for any value of a.
1. a and b form a linear pair, so b = 180 − 35 = 145.
2. a and d form a linear pair, so d = 180 − 35 = 145.
3. For any a: b = 180 − a and d = 180 − a, so b and d are equal whatever a is.
4. In the same way, c = 180 − b = a, so a and c are equal. This justification is a proof.
Answer: b = 145° and d = 145°; vertically opposite angles are always equal

1. a and b form a linear pair, so b = 180 − 35 = 145.
2. a and d form a linear pair, so d = 180 − 35 = 145.
3. For any a: b = 180 − a and d = 180 − a, so b and d are equal whatever a is.
4. In the same way, c = 180 − b = a, so a and c are equal. This justification is a proof.
Answer: b = 145° and d = 145°; vertically opposite angles are always equal

content.text:
Neighbouring angles at a crossing make a linear pair and add to 180 degrees.
Angles that face each other are vertically opposite and equal.
One angle gives the other three: subtract it from 180 for the neighbours and copy it to the one opposite.

concepts.concept_name: Figure it Out (intersecting lines), Q1

content.text:
Figure it Out (intersecting lines), Q1: Two lines l and m cross, and the four angles are named a, b, c and d going round the crossing, with a and b neighbours. List all the linear pairs and all the pairs of vertically opposite angles.
1. Linear pairs are neighbouring angles that sit on a straight line: a and b, b and c, c and d, d and a.
2. Vertically opposite angles face each other across the crossing: a and c, b and d.
3. Check: going round, there are four neighbouring pairs and two facing pairs.
Answer: Linear pairs: a and b, b and c, c and d, d and a. Vertically opposite pairs: a and c, b and d

concepts.concept_name: Measuring and reasoning are not the same

content.text:
You might have noticed that when you measure linear pairs, sometimes they may not add up to 180°. Or, when you measure vertically opposite angles they may be unequal sometimes. What are the reasons for this?
There could be different reasons: measurement errors because of improper use of measuring instruments, in this case, a protractor; and variation in the thickness of the lines drawn. The “ideal” line in geometry does not have any thickness! But it is not possible for us to draw lines without any thickness.
In geometry, we create ideal versions of “lines” and other shapes we see around us, and analyse the relationships between them. For example, we know that the angle formed by a straight line is 180°. So, if another line divides this angle into two parts, both parts should add up to 180°. We arrive at this by reasoning and not by measurement. When we measure, it might not be exactly so, for the reasons mentioned above. Still the measurements come out very close to what we predict, because of which geometry finds widespread application in different disciplines such as physics, art, engineering and architecture.

1. Predict first: one pair measures 63° and 119°; do they break the rule of 180°?

3. The rule comes from a straight line, an ideal line with no thickness, so reasoning gives the exact value and measuring gives a close value.

content.text:
Worked example: Imran measures a linear pair as 63° and 119°. Their sum is not 180°. Does that break the rule? What should the second angle be?
1. 63 + 119 = 182, which is 2° more than 180.
2. The rule of 180° comes from a straight line with no thickness; a drawn line is thick and the reading of a protractor can be off by a degree or two.
3. By reasoning, the second angle is 180 − 63 = 117.
4. So the measure 119° is 2° off, a measurement error, and the rule is not broken.
Answer: No; the second angle should be 117°, and the 2° is a measurement error

concepts.concept_name: All four angles equal: perpendicular lines

content.text:
Can you draw a pair of intersecting lines such that all four angles are equal? Can you figure out what will be the measure of each angle?
If two lines intersect and all four angles are equal, then each angle must be a right angle (90°).
Perpendicular lines are a pair of lines which intersect each other at right angles (90°). Lines l and m in the figure are perpendicular to each other.

content.text:
Worked example: Two lines cross so that all four angles are equal. Find each angle, and say what the lines are called.
1. Two neighbouring angles are a linear pair, so together they are 180°.
2. They are equal, so each is 180 ÷ 2 = 90.
3. All four angles are 90°, that is, right angles.
4. Lines that intersect at right angles are perpendicular, however the pair is tilted.
Answer: Each angle is 90°, and the lines are perpendicular

MATHEMATICAL IMAGE REQUIREMENT
Teaching purpose: Show two tilted lines that cross so that all four angles are 90 degrees, so tilt does not matter.

Composition: Flat, friendly educational illustration for a middle-school maths lesson: plain white background, thin uniform dark outlines (#2B2B2B), flat fills with no shading and no gradients, clean sans-serif labels in plain classroom English a child can read aloud. Colour-blind-safe colours: #009E73 for a positive/first idea, #D55E00 for a negative/contrasting idea, #0072B2 for a first set or step, #E69F00 for a second set or step, #CC79A7 for the focus or highlight, #6B7280 for construction lines and for anything struck out. 16:9 landscape, 1456 by 816 pixels. Keep it uncluttered: one main idea per frame, a single clear focal object, generous white space around it, large readable labels, nothing decorative that does not teach. Two long tilted lines crossing at the centre of a white frame, with a small square mark in each of the four corners.

Exact mathematical structure:
- Line l (teal #0072B2) tilted about 30 degrees above the horizontal, rising to the right.
- Line m (amber #E69F00) crossing l at the centre point at exactly 90 degrees, so it falls to the right at about 60 degrees below the horizontal.
- Four small squares, one in each of the four angles at the crossing, each filled light reddish purple (#CC79A7).
- Each of the four angles is labelled 90 degrees, close to the corner.
- Neither line is horizontal or vertical.
- Line names l and m sit at the far ends.

Visible text:
- l
- m
- 90°
- 90°
- 90°
- 90°

Critical rejection conditions:
- any angle not drawn as a right angle
- a horizontal or vertical line
- fewer or more than 4 square marks
- any count of objects, cells, ticks or rows that differs from the numbers stated in the spec
- any text beyond the listed visible text, or any listed text misspelled or altered
- any board name, publisher name, book title, page number or curriculum branding anywhere in the frame
- a hyphen used in place of a minus sign on any labelled number

content.text:
1. Predict first: two segments that share one end, two that cross near their middles, and two that run side by side, which of them will meet if you extend them?
2. Use the words: a point where they meet, an endpoint, the midpoint, meet, intersect, and read the angle.
3. Segments that lean even a little towards each other meet when extended far enough; segments that keep the same gap do not seem likely to.

content.text:
Worked example: Five pairs of segments are drawn. FG and FH share the end F, with 115.3° between them. AB and CD cross at X, at about 60°, a little past the middle of each. IJ and LM cross at Y, at about 80°, close to the middle of both. Describe each pair in mathematical words.
1. FG and FH meet at the endpoint F, at an angle of 115.3°.
2. AB and CD intersect at the point X, at an angle of about 60°. X is not the midpoint of either segment.
3. IJ and LM intersect at the point Y, at an angle of about 80°. Y is close to the midpoint of both segments.
4. The 60° and 80° are measured, so they are close values, as the earlier topic explained.
Answer: FG and FH meet at the endpoint F at 115.3°; AB and CD intersect at X at about 60°; IJ and LM intersect close to both midpoints at about 80°

concepts.concept_name: Do the segments meet, cross or stay apart?

content.text:
Worked example: Two more pairs are drawn: ST and UV lean towards each other by about 2.5° and look nearly side by side; OP and QR keep about the same gap along their whole length. Are ST and UV likely to meet if extended? Are OP and QR?
1. ST and UV lean towards each other, so far beyond T and V they would meet, about four lengths of the segment beyond the ends.
2. OP and QR keep the same gap from one end to the other, so they are not likely to meet.
3. By eye we can only guess for lines this close, so we will need a sure test.
Answer: ST and UV would meet if extended far enough; OP and QR are not likely to meet

concepts.concept_name: Parallel lines, in pictures and around us

content.text:
Here are some examples of lines we notice around us. What is common to the lines in the pictures? They do not seem likely to intersect each other. Such lines are called parallel lines.
Parallel lines are a pair of lines that lie on the same plane, and do not meet however far we extend them at both ends.
Name some parallel lines you can spot in your classroom.
Parallel lines are often used in artwork and shading.
Which pairs of lines appear to be parallel in the figure of nine segments?
Note: It is important that the lines lie on the same plane. A line drawn on a table and a line drawn on the board may never meet but that does not make them parallel.

1. Predict first: the two long edges of a ruler, a railway track, the top and bottom of a window; which pairs of lines in your classroom stay the same gap apart?
2. Parallel needs two things together: the lines lie on one plane, and they never meet however far they are extended in both directions.
3. A line on a table and a line on the board may never meet but they lie on different planes, so they are not parallel.

content.text:
Worked example: Nine segments a to i are drawn on a grid. a, h and i are upright. c and g are flat. d and f lean one way, each along the diagonal of a square. b and e lean the other way, also along the diagonal of a square. Which pairs of lines appear to be parallel?
1. Upright segments: a, h and i keep the same gap, so they appear parallel to each other.
2. Flat segments: c and g appear parallel to each other.
3. Segments leaning one way: d and f appear parallel to each other.
4. Segments leaning the other way: b and e appear parallel to each other.
5. A flat segment and an upright one cross; they are not parallel.
Answer: a, h and i; c and g; d and f; b and e

concepts.concept_name: Folding a sheet in half again and again

content.text:
Activity 2: Use a plain square sheet of paper (use a newspaper for this activity).
How would you describe the opposite edges of the sheet? They are parallel to each other.
How would you describe the adjacent edges of the sheet? The adjacent edges are perpendicular to each other. They meet at a point. They form right angles.
Fold the sheet horizontally in half. A new line is formed. How many parallel lines do you see now? How does the new line segment relate to the vertical sides?
Make one more horizontal fold in the folded sheet. How many parallel lines do you see now?
What will happen if you do it once more? How many parallel lines will you get? Is there a pattern? Check if the pattern extends further, if you make another horizontal fold.

content.text:
1. Predict first: after one fold in half, how many parallel lines does the sheet have, counting its two edges?
2. The two original edges and the first crease give three parallel lines, and the crease is perpendicular to the upright sides.
3. Each fold in half splits every gap into two, so the number of gaps doubles and the lines are one more than the gaps.

content.text:
Worked example: A square sheet has two flat edges. Fold it horizontally in half again and again. Count the parallel lines, including the two edges, after one, two, three and four folds. What is the pattern?
1. Opposite edges are parallel, and adjacent edges are perpendicular.
2. After 1 fold there are 2 gaps, so 2 + 1 = 3 parallel lines.
3. After 2 folds there are 4 gaps, so 4 + 1 = 5 parallel lines.
4. After 3 folds there are 8 gaps, so 8 + 1 = 9 parallel lines.
5. After 4 folds there are 16 gaps, so 16 + 1 = 17 parallel lines.
6. Every fold doubles the gaps, so the number of lines is 1 more than the gaps, 3, 5, 9, 17, ...
Answer: 3, 5, 9 and 17 parallel lines; the gaps double and the lines are one more than the gaps

concepts.concept_name: Perpendicular and parallel folds

content.text:
Make a vertical fold in the square sheet. This new vertical line is perpendicular to the previous horizontal lines.
Fold the sheet along a diagonal. Can you find a fold that creates a line parallel to the diagonal line?
Here is another activity for you to try. Fold a square sheet of paper in the middle and unfold it. Fold the edges towards the centre line and unfold them. Fold the top right and bottom left corners onto the creased line to create triangles. The triangles should not cross the crease lines.
Are a, b and c parallel to p, q and r respectively? Why or why not?

1. Predict first: if you fold a sheet along a diagonal, where would a second crease run to be parallel to it?
2. A vertical fold across flat lines meets each of them at 90°.
3. A fold that puts one corner on the centre of the sheet makes a crease at right angles to the other diagonal, so it is parallel to the first diagonal.

content.text:
Worked example: Fold a square sheet along one diagonal. Describe a fold that makes a line parallel to this diagonal and say why it is parallel.
1. Fold the corner that is not on the diagonal onto the centre of the sheet.
2. The crease is at right angles to the other diagonal, because the fold sends the corner straight along it to the centre.
3. The first diagonal is also at right angles to the other diagonal.
4. Two lines at right angles to the same line are parallel, so the crease is parallel to the diagonal.
Answer: Fold a corner onto the centre; the crease is parallel to the diagonal

concepts.concept_name: Perpendicular and parallel folds

content.text:
Worked example: A square sheet is folded in the middle both ways, the edges are folded to the centre line, and then two opposite corners are folded onto a centre crease to make triangles. Pairs of creases a and p, b and q, c and r are marked. Are they parallel?
1. a and p lie along folds that run the same way, so they lie on parallel lines.
2. b and q are both perpendicular to those lines, so b and q are parallel to each other.
3. c and r are the slanting edges of the two folded triangles. Both triangular folds are made against the same diagonal direction, so c and r are parallel.
4. So a is parallel to p, b to q, and c to r.
Answer: Yes: a is parallel to p, b to q and c to r

concepts.concept_name: Arrow marks and the square: notation

content.text:
Notations
In mathematics, we use an arrow mark (>) to show that a set of lines is parallel. If there is more than one set of parallel lines, the second set is shown with two arrow marks and so on. Perpendicular lines are marked with a square angle between them.

content.text:
1. Predict first: if a drawing has two different sets of parallel lines, how could we tell them apart without using colours?
2. One arrow mark on each line of the first set, two arrow marks on each line of the second set.
3. A small square in the corner between two lines shows a right angle.

content.text:
Worked example: A drawing has two flat parallel lines, two slanting parallel lines, and one upright line that crosses a flat line at 90°. How are these marked?
1. The flat parallel lines are the first set: one arrow mark on each.
2. The slanting parallel lines are the second set: two arrow marks on each.
3. The upright line and the flat line are perpendicular: a small square in the corner between them.
4. The 90° is not written out; the square says it.
Answer: One arrow on each flat line, two arrows on each slanting line, and a square at the right angle

concepts.concept_name: Practice: parallel and perpendicular on dot paper

content.text:
On dot paper a line has steps across and steps up.
A parallel line repeats the same steps; a perpendicular line swaps the steps and changes one sign.
Mark parallel lines with arrow marks, and a right angle with a square.

tool_config.title: Dot Paper Line Studio
tool_config.idea: On dot paper a line is described by its steps across and up. Equal steps make parallel lines; swapping the steps and changing one sign makes a perpendicular line.
tool_config.screen: A grid of dots up to 13 by 13. The student joins two dots to draw a segment between dots. A readout shows the steps across and up of the last segment. A mode switch asks for a parallel, a perpendicular, or a yes-or-no test for a pair of segments. Arrow marks and a square are added automatically to a correct pair.
student_does: Read the task card: draw a parallel, draw a perpendicular, or decide for a pair.
Join dots to draw the segment and read its steps.
Draw the new segment and press Check.
Move a dot of the new segment and watch the steps readout.
challenges: A flat segment: draw a perpendicular (an upright segment).
A segment with steps 2 across and 2 up: draw a perpendicular (2 across and 2 down).
A segment with steps 1 across and 3 up: draw a parallel (1 across and 3 up from another dot).
A segment with steps 2 across and 3 up: try a perpendicular (3 across and 2 down), and say how wide the grid must be to hold it (at least 4 dots across).
Do segments with steps 3 across and 3 down, and 1 across and 1 down, lie on parallel lines (no, they lean opposite ways).
Do segments with steps 5 across and 2 up, and 10 across and 4 up, lie on parallel lines (yes, 5 times 4 is 2 times 10).
Draw lines parallel to a 4 by 4 diagonal, a 1 by 6 steep segment and a 5 by 2 shallow segment.
feedback: A segment that does not repeat the steps shows both segments on a shared grid with the steps written on each, and the mismatch is circled.
A perpendicular that has the right steps but different lengths is accepted, with a note that length does not matter.
A drawn pair that looks parallel but whose steps differ is shown extended until the lines cross.
tool_config.done_when: Seven tasks are completed, each checked by the steps across and up.

concepts.concept_name: Figure it Out (parallel and perpendicular lines), Q1

content.text:
Figure it Out (parallel and perpendicular lines), Q1: Draw some lines perpendicular to the lines given on the dot paper. There are two grids, each 3 dots across and 4 dots up. In the left grid, one segment is flat, 2 steps long, and another leans with 2 steps across and 2 steps up. In the right grid, one segment has 2 steps across and 3 steps down, and another is upright, 2 steps long.
1. Flat segment: an upright segment is perpendicular to it, so draw upright segments between dots (0 steps across, some steps up).
2. Leaning segment with 2 across and 2 up: swap the steps and change one sign, giving 2 across and 2 down. Draw leaning segments of 2 across and 2 down.
3. Upright segment: a flat segment is perpendicular to it, so draw flat segments between dots.
4. Segment with 2 across and 3 down: the perpendicular needs 3 across and 2 up, and the grid is only 3 dots, that is 2 steps, across. It cannot be drawn between dots on this grid, so it needs a wider grid or a set square.
5. Perpendicular lines need not be one flat and one upright: the leaning ones also meet at 90°.
Answer: Upright lines for the flat segment, flat lines for the upright one, lines of 2 across and 2 down for the leaning one; the 2-across-3-down segment needs a wider grid

concepts.concept_name: Figure it Out (parallel and perpendicular lines), Q2

content.text:
Figure it Out (parallel and perpendicular lines), Q2: Five shapes are drawn on a dot grid. Each corner is given as (across, down) from the top left. Shape 1: (0,0), (2,2), (2,4), (3,5), (0,5). Shape 2: (6,1), (10,1), (8,3), (4,3). Shape 3: (5,4), (7,6), (7,8), (5,8), (3,6), (5,6). Shape 4: (0,7), (3,7), (0,10). Shape 5: (5,9), (8,9), (11,7), (11,11), (5,11). Mark the parallel lines with arrow marks (a single arrow, double arrow and so on) and the angle between perpendicular lines with a square. (a) How did you spot the perpendicular lines? (b) How did you spot the parallel lines?
1. Shape 1: the side (0,0) to (2,2) and the side (2,4) to (3,5) both go 1 across and 1 down in each step, so they are parallel (single arrow). The upright sides (2,2) to (2,4) and (0,5) to (0,0) are parallel (double arrow). One right angle, at (0,5), between the upright side and the flat bottom.
2. Shape 2: (6,1) to (10,1) and (8,3) to (4,3) are both flat, so parallel (single arrow). (10,1) to (8,3) and (4,3) to (6,1) both go 2 across and 2 down, so parallel (double arrow). No right angle.
3. Shape 3: three pairs. (5,4) to (7,6) with (5,8) to (3,6) (single arrow). (7,6) to (7,8) with (5,6) to (5,4) (double arrow). (7,8) to (5,8) with (3,6) to (5,6) (triple arrow). Right angles at (7,8) and at (5,6).
4. Shape 4: only one right angle, at (0,7), between the flat side and the upright side. No pair of parallel sides.
5. Shape 5: (5,9) to (8,9) with (11,11) to (5,11) are flat, parallel (single arrow). (11,7) to (11,11) with (5,11) to (5,9) are upright, parallel (double arrow). Right angles at (5,9), (5,11) and (11,11).
6. (a) Perpendicular lines: a flat line and an upright line on the grid meet at a right angle.
7. (b) Parallel lines: segments that repeat the same steps across and down, so the gap between them stays the same.
Answer: Shape 1: two pairs parallel and one right angle; shape 2: two pairs; shape 3: three pairs and two right angles; shape 4: one right angle; shape 5: two pairs and three right angles. (a) Flat and upright lines meet at 90°. (b) Same steps, same gap

concepts.concept_name: Figure it Out (parallel and perpendicular lines), Q3

content.text:
Figure it Out (parallel and perpendicular lines), Q3: On dot paper, draw different sets of parallel lines. The line segments can be of different lengths but should have dots as endpoints.
1. Flat sets: draw two or three flat segments in different rows; they can have different lengths.
2. Upright sets: draw two or three upright segments in different columns.
3. Leaning sets: start at different dots and take the same steps, for example 1 across and 1 up, or 2 across and 1 up, each time.
4. Check each set: the steps are the same, so the lines keep the same gap and are parallel.
Answer: Sets of flat lines, upright lines and leaning lines that repeat the same steps, such as 1 across and 1 up, or 2 across and 1 up

concepts.concept_name: Figure it Out (parallel and perpendicular lines), Q4

content.text:
Figure it Out (parallel and perpendicular lines), Q4: Using your sense of how parallel lines look, draw lines parallel to the line segments a to h on dot paper (13 dots by 13 dots). Taking steps across to the right and then up or down: a is 1 across, 1 down; b is 2 across, 2 down; c is 3 across, 3 up; d is 4 across, 4 up; e is 1 across, 3 down; f is 1 across, 6 down; g is 5 across, 2 up; h is 10 across, 3 down. (a) Did you find it challenging to draw some of them? (b) Which ones? (c) How did you do it?
1. a, b, c and d lean at the diagonal of a square, so they are easy to copy by eye.
2. e, f, g and h have unusual steps, so they are harder to draw by eye.
3. Method: count the steps across and up of the given segment, start at a new dot, and take the same steps. For e: 1 across and 3 down; for f: 1 across and 6 down; for g: 5 across and 2 up; for h: 10 across and 3 down.
4. Because the steps are the same, the new segment keeps the same gap and is parallel.
Answer: (a) Yes. (b) The segments e, f, g and h. (c) Count the steps across and up and repeat them from another dot

concepts.concept_name: Figure it Out (parallel and perpendicular lines), Q5

content.text:
Figure it Out (parallel and perpendicular lines), Q5: Which line is parallel to line a, line b or line c? How do you decide this? Line a, line b and line c lean to the right. A steep line meets a at one end and b and c at its other end. The angles the steep line makes are about 30° with a, about 29° with c and about 33° with b.
1. Compare the angles the steep line makes: with a it is about 30°, with c about 29°, with b about 33°.
2. The angle with c is close to the angle with a; the angle with b is 3° more.
3. Equal corresponding angles mean parallel, so c is the line parallel to a.
4. Another way to see it: c stays the same gap from a, while b closes in.
Answer: Line c is parallel to line a, because the angles made with the steep line are about equal, 30° and 29°

media.description: Five shapes are drawn on a dot grid. The board marks parallel sides with one, two or three arrows and right angles with a square, shape by shape, and then says how to spot each kind of line.

concepts.concept_name: A transversal and its eight angles

content.text:
We saw what happens when two lines intersect in different ways. Let us explore what happens when one line intersects two different lines.
In the figure, line t intersects lines l and m. t is called a transversal. Notice that 8 angles are formed when a line crosses a pair of lines.
Is it possible for all the eight angles to have different measurements? Why, why not?
What about five different angles, 6, 5, 4, 3 and 2?
Since ∠1 and ∠3 are vertically opposite angles, they are equal. Are there other pairs of vertically opposite angles? We can see that there are a total of four pairs of vertically opposite angles and in each pair, the angles are equal to each other.
Thus, when a transversal intersects two lines, it forms eight angles with a maximum of four distinct angle measures.

content.text:
1. Predict first: a line crosses two lines; how many angles are made, and how many different sizes could there be?
2. Each crossing makes four angles, and there are two crossings, so eight angles.
3. Each crossing gives two pairs of vertically opposite angles, and each pair is equal, so there are four pairs in all.

content.text:
Worked example: A transversal t crosses lines l and m. The angles are numbered 1, 2, 3, 4 going round the crossing with l, and 5, 6, 7, 8 going round the crossing with m in the same way, so that 1 and 3, 2 and 4, 5 and 7, 6 and 8 are vertically opposite. Can all eight angles have different measures? Can the five angles 6, 5, 4, 3 and 2 be all different?
1. Vertically opposite angles are equal: angle 1 equals angle 3, 2 equals 4, 5 equals 7 and 6 equals 8.
2. There are four pairs, so there are at most 4 different measures, and all eight cannot differ.
3. Among the five angles 6, 5, 4, 3 and 2, the angles 2 and 4 are a vertically opposite pair, so they are equal.
4. So these five angles cannot all be different.
Answer: No: at most four different measures; and 2 and 4 are equal, so the five cannot all be different

concepts.concept_name: Corresponding angles

content.text:
In the figure, we notice that the transversal t forms two sets of angles, one with line l and another with line m. There are angles in the first set that correspond to angles in the second set based on their position.
∠1 and ∠5 are called corresponding angles. Similarly, ∠2 and ∠6, ∠3 and ∠7, ∠4 and ∠8 are the corresponding angles formed when transversal t intersects lines l and m.

2. Corresponding angles are in the same corner at the two crossings.
3. Each angle in the first set has exactly one corresponding angle in the second set.

content.text:
Worked example: In the transversal figure, 1, 2, 3, 4 are at the crossing with l and 5, 6, 7, 8 at the crossing with m, with 1 and 5 in the same corner. Name the corresponding angle of each of 2, 3 and 4.
1. The corresponding angle is in the same corner at the other crossing.
2. 2 is in the same corner as 6, so 2 and 6 are corresponding.
3. 3 is in the same corner as 7, so 3 and 7 are corresponding.
4. 4 is in the same corner as 8, so 4 and 8 are corresponding.
Answer: 2 and 6, 3 and 7, 4 and 8

Colour-blind-safe colours: #009E73 for a positive/first idea, #D55E00 for a negative/contrasting idea, #0072B2 for a first set or step, #E69F00 for a second set or step, #CC79A7 for the focus or highlight, #6B7280 for construction lines and for anything struck out. 16:9 landscape, 1456 by 816 pixels. Keep it uncluttered: one main idea per frame, a single clear focal object, generous white space around it, large readable labels, nothing decorative that does not teach. The same two-lines-and-transversal figure, with only one corresponding pair emphasised and the rest faint.

Exact mathematical structure:
- Two horizontal grey (#6B7280) lines l above and m below, and one slanting dark line t crossing both.
- At the crossing with l, the top left angle is filled reddish purple (#CC79A7) and numbered 1.
- At the crossing with m, the top left angle is filled reddish purple (#CC79A7) and numbered 5.
- A dashed grey arrow runs down along t from angle 1 to angle 5.
- The other six angles are drawn only as thin grey arcs with no number and no fill.
- A short caption sits at the right side beside the dashed arrow.

Visible text:
- l
- m
- t
- 1

- same corner

- any of the other six angles filled or numbered
- 1 and 5 in different corners (for example 5 at the bottom right)

concepts.concept_name: Drawing lines with equal corresponding angles

content.text:
Activity 3: Draw a pair of lines and a transversal such that they form two distinct angles.
Step 1: Draw a line l and a transversal t intersecting it at point X.
Step 2: Measure ∠a formed by lines l and t (let us say it is 60°). How many distinct angles have formed now? If one angle is 60°, the other angle of the linear pair should be 120°. So, we already have two distinct angles. So, when we draw another line intersecting the transversal t we wish to form only two angles, 60° and 120°.
Step 3: Mark a point Y on line t.
Step 4: Draw a line m through point Y that forms a 60° angle to line t. This can be done either by copying ∠a with a tracing paper or you can use a protractor to measure the angles.
What do you observe about lines l and m? Do they appear to be parallel to each other? Yes, they do appear to be parallel to each other. Angles ∠a and ∠b are corresponding angles formed by the transversal t on lines l and m. These corresponding angles are equal to each other.
When the corresponding angles formed by a transversal on a pair of lines are equal to each other, then the pair of lines are parallel to each other.

content.text:
Worked example: A line l and a transversal t meet at X, and the angle a between them is 60°. Describe how to draw a line m through a point Y on t that is parallel to l, and name the angles that are equal.
1. The other angle of the linear pair at X is 180 − 60 = 120, so there are two distinct angles, 60° and 120°.
2. Mark a point Y on t.
3. Draw a line m through Y that makes a 60° angle with t, on the same side as a, by copying a on tracing paper or with a protractor.
4. The angle b at Y is 60° and a at X is 60°; they are corresponding angles, and they are equal.
5. So l and m are parallel.
Answer: m is parallel to l, since the corresponding angles a and b are both 60°

content.text:
Suppose, we have a transversal intersecting two parallel lines. What can be said about the corresponding angles?
Activity 4: The figure has a pair of parallel lines l and m (what is the notation used in the figure to indicate they are parallel?). Line t is the transversal across these two lines. ∠a and ∠b are corresponding angles. Trace ∠a on a tracing paper. Now place this tracing paper over ∠b and see if the angles align exactly. You will observe that the angles match. Check the other corresponding angles in the figure using a protractor. Are all the corresponding angles equal to each other?
Corresponding angles formed by a transversal intersecting a pair of parallel lines are always equal to each other.

content.text:
Worked example: Lines l and m are parallel, with arrow marks, and t crosses both. The angle a at l is 65°, and b is its corresponding angle at m. Find b and the other three pairs of corresponding angles.
1. a and b are corresponding angles of parallel lines, so b = 65°.
2. The angle next to a on the straight line is 180 − 65 = 115, and its corresponding angle is also 115°.
3. So of the four pairs of corresponding angles, two pairs are 65° and two pairs are 115°.
4. Each pair is equal, because the lines are parallel.
Answer: b = 65°; the four pairs of corresponding angles are 65°, 65°, 115° and 115°

content.text:
Worked example: Two lines l and m lean 10° apart, so they are not parallel. A transversal t makes 30° with l, and m leans 10° more towards t than l does, so t makes 20° with m on the matching side. Can the two corresponding angles be made equal by turning t?
1. The corresponding angles are 30° and 20°, and 30 − 20 = 10.
2. Turn t to make 50° with l; then it makes 40° with m, and 50 − 40 = 10.
3. Each time the two angles differ by 10°, because the lines lean 10° apart.
4. So no transversal makes them equal: corresponding angles of lines that are not parallel are never equal.
Answer: No; the corresponding angles always differ by 10°

concepts.concept_name: Sliding a set square along a ruler

content.text:
Can you draw a pair of parallel lines using a ruler and a set square?
Draw a line l with a scale. By sliding your set square you can make two lines perpendicular to line l.
Are these two lines parallel to each other? How are we sure that they are parallel to each other? What angles are formed between these lines and line l?
Since we used a set square, the angles measure 90°. The position of the lines is different, but they make the same angle with l. If line l is seen as a transversal to the two new lines, then the corresponding angles measure 90°. As we know these are corresponding angles and they are equal, we can be sure that the lines are parallel.
Draw two more parallel lines using the long side of the set square.
How do you know these two lines are parallel? Can you check if the corresponding angles are equal?
Note: Encourage checking the equality of corresponding angles both by using the tracing method and using protractors to measure the angles. Pay attention to the language used to make the relationship between corresponding angles and parallel lines. Equality of corresponding angles is both necessary and sufficient for the pair of lines to be parallel to each other.

content.text:
1. Predict first: you slide a set square along a ruler and draw along one edge twice; will the two lines be parallel?
2. The set square does not turn while it slides, so it makes the same angle with the ruler every time.
3. Equal corresponding angles are both a test and a guarantee: they give parallel lines, and parallel lines give them.

content.text:
Worked example: Draw a line l with a ruler. Slide a set square along l and draw two lines along its upright edge. Are the two lines parallel? Which angles prove it?
1. The upright edge of the set square makes a 90° angle with l each time it is drawn.
2. Seen with l as the transversal, the two angles of 90° are corresponding angles.
3. The corresponding angles are equal, both 90°.
4. So the two lines are parallel.
Answer: Yes, parallel: the corresponding angles are both 90°

concepts.concept_name: Sliding a set square along a ruler

content.text:
Worked example: Place the long side of a 45° set square so that it makes 45° with l, and draw along it, then slide and draw again. Are the two lines parallel? How can you check?
1. The long side makes 45° with l each time, because the set square does not turn.
2. The two angles of 45° are corresponding angles of the transversal l.
3. They are equal, so the lines are parallel.
4. To check, trace one angle and slide the tracing over the other, or measure both with a protractor.
Answer: Yes, parallel: the corresponding angles are both 45°

concepts.concept_name: A parallel line through a point, by folding

content.text:
Making Parallel Lines through Paper Folding
Let us try to do the same with paper folding. For a line l (given as a crease), how do we make a line parallel to l such that it passes through point A?
We know how to fold a piece of paper to get a line perpendicular to l. Now, try to fold a perpendicular to l such that it passes through point A. Let us call this new crease t.
Now, fold a line perpendicular to t passing through A again. Let us call this line m. The lines l and m are parallel to each other.
Why are lines l and m parallel to each other?

content.text:
Worked example: A crease l and a point A are given. Fold a line m through A parallel to l, and say why it is parallel.
1. Fold the paper so that l falls on itself and the crease passes through A. This crease t is perpendicular to l.
2. Unfold. Now fold the paper so that t falls on itself and the new crease passes through A. This crease is m, perpendicular to t.
3. t crosses l at 90° and crosses m at 90°, and these are corresponding angles.
4. The corresponding angles are equal, so l and m are parallel.
Answer: m is parallel to l, since both are perpendicular to t, so the corresponding angles are both 90°

concepts.concept_name: Figure it Out (drawing parallel lines), Q1

content.text:
Figure it Out (drawing parallel lines), Q1: Can you draw a line parallel to l that goes through the point A? How will you do it with the tools from your geometry box? Describe your method.
1. You need a ruler, a set square, a pencil and an eraser.
2. Place the set square so that one side lies along l.
3. Hold the ruler against another side of the set square, so that the ruler will not move.
4. Slide the set square along the ruler until the side that was along l reaches the point A.
5. Draw a line along that side, through A.
6. This line is parallel to l: the set square did not turn, so it made the same angle with the ruler, and the corresponding angles are equal.
Answer: Slide the set square along a ruler until its side reaches A and draw along it; the line through A is parallel to l

concepts.concept_name: Reaching the alternate angle in two moves

content.text:
In the figure, ∠d is called the alternate angle of ∠f, and ∠c is the alternate angle of ∠e.
You can find the alternate angle of a given angle, say ∠f, by first finding the corresponding angle of ∠f, which is ∠b and then finding the vertically opposite angle of ∠b, which is ∠d.
Activity 6: If ∠f is 120° what is the measure of its alternate angle ∠d?
We can find the measure of ∠d if we know ∠b because they are vertically opposite angles. Remember, vertically opposite angles are equal. What is the measure of ∠b? It is 120° because it is the corresponding angle of ∠f. So, ∠d also measures 120°.
In fact, ∠f = ∠b irrespective of the measure of ∠f. Why? Because ∠b is the corresponding angle of ∠f. Similarly, ∠b = ∠d irrespective of the measure of ∠b. Why? Because ∠d is the vertically opposite angle of ∠b. So, it must always be the case that ∠f = ∠d.
Using our understanding of corresponding angles without any measurements, we have justified that alternate angles are always equal.
Alternate angles formed by a transversal intersecting a pair of parallel lines are always equal to each other.

content.text:
Worked example: Lines l and m are parallel and t is a transversal. The angles a, b, d, c are at the upper crossing (a top left, b top right, d bottom left, c bottom right), and e, f, h, g are in the same corners at the lower crossing. If f is 120°, find its alternate angle d.
1. First move: b is the corresponding angle of f, so b = 120°.
2. Second move: d is the vertically opposite angle of b, so d = 120°.
3. So f = d = 120°, whatever the size of f.
4. Alternate angles are equal when the lines are parallel.
Answer: d = 120°, so alternate angles of parallel lines are equal

concepts.concept_name: All eight angles from one

content.text:
Example 1: Parallel lines l and m are intersected by the transversal t. If ∠6 is 135°, what are the measures of the other angles?
Solution: ∠6 is 135°, so ∠2 is also 135°, because it is the corresponding angle of ∠6 and the lines l and m are parallel.
∠8 is 135°, because it is the vertically opposite angle of ∠6. ∠4 is 135° because it is the corresponding angle of ∠8. ∠2 is 135° because it is the vertically opposite angle of ∠4. So, ∠2, ∠4, ∠6, and ∠8 are all 135°.
∠5 and ∠6 are a linear pair, together they measure 180°. If ∠6 is 135°, then ∠5 is 180 − 135 = 45°. We can similarly find out that ∠1, ∠3, and ∠7 measure 45°.

content.text:
Worked example: Lines l and m are parallel and t is a transversal. The angles 1, 2, 3, 4 go round the crossing with l and 5, 6, 7, 8 round the crossing with m in the same corners, so 2 and 6 correspond, and 6 and 8 are vertically opposite, and 5 and 6 are a linear pair. If angle 6 is 135°, find the other angles.
1. Angle 2 is the corresponding angle of 6, so angle 2 is 135°.
2. Angle 8 is vertically opposite to 6, so it is 135°; angle 4 is the corresponding angle of 8, so it is 135°.
3. So angles 2, 4, 6 and 8 are all 135°.
4. Angles 5 and 6 are a linear pair, so angle 5 is 180 − 135 = 45.
5. In the same way angles 1, 3 and 7 are 45°.
Answer: Angles 2, 4, 6 and 8 are 135°; angles 1, 3, 5 and 7 are 45°

concepts.concept_name: Testing a pair of lines with an alternate angle

content.text:
Example 2: Lines l and m are intersected by the transversal t. If ∠a is 120° and ∠f is 70°, are lines l and m parallel to each other?
Solution: ∠a is 120°, so ∠b is 60° because ∠a and ∠b form a linear pair. ∠b is a corresponding angle of ∠f. If l and m are parallel, ∠b should be equal to ∠f, however, they are not equal.
Therefore, lines l and m are not parallel to each other as the corresponding angles formed by the transversal t are not equal to each other.

content.text:
Worked example: Lines l and m are cut by a transversal t, with the angles a, b, d, c at the upper crossing and e, f, h, g in the same corners at the lower crossing. The angle a is 120° and the angle f is 70°. Are l and m parallel?
1. a and b are a linear pair, so b = 180 − 120 = 60.
2. b and f are corresponding angles. If l and m were parallel, b would be equal to f.
3. But b = 60° and f = 70°, which are not equal, as 70 − 60 = 10.
4. So l and m are not parallel.
Answer: No: the corresponding angles are 60° and 70°, which are not equal

concepts.concept_name: Interior angles on the same side

content.text:
Example 3: Parallel lines l and m are intersected by the transversal t. If ∠3 is 50°, what is the measure of ∠6?
Solution: ∠3 is 50°; therefore, ∠2 is 130°, because ∠2 and ∠3 form a linear pair, and linear pairs always add up to 180°. ∠2 and ∠6 are corresponding angles, and they need to be equal since lines l and m are parallel. So, ∠6 is 130°.
Angles ∠3 and ∠6 are called interior angles.
Is there a relation between ∠3 and ∠6? You could try to find the relationship by taking different values for ∠3 and see what ∠6 is. Once you find a relation, try to justify it or prove that this relation holds always. You will find that the sum of the interior angles on the same side of the transversal always add up to 180°.

lines: Example 3: Parallel lines l and m are intersected by the transversal t. If ∠3 is 50°, what is the measure of ∠6?

Solution: ∠3 is 50°; therefore, ∠2 is 130°, because ∠2 and ∠3 form a linear pair, and linear pairs always add up to 180°. ∠2 and ∠6 are corresponding angles, and they need to be equal since lines l and m are parallel. So, ∠6 is 130°.
Angles ∠3 and ∠6 are called interior angles.

content.text:
Example 4: Line segment AB is parallel to CD and AD is parallel to BC. ∠DAC is 65° and ∠ADC is 60°. What are the measures of angles ∠CAB, ∠ABC, and ∠BCD?
Solution: Let us observe the parallel lines AB and CD. AD is a transversal of these two lines.
We know that the sum of the interior angles formed by a transversal on a pair of parallel lines adds up to 180°. So ∠ADC + ∠DAB = 180°. 60° + ∠DAB = 180°. So ∠DAB = 120°.
Can we find ∠CAB from this? ∠DAB = ∠DAC + ∠CAB. So 120° = 65° + ∠CAB. So ∠CAB = 55°.
Let us observe the parallel line segments AD and BC. They are intersected by a transversal CD. So, ∠ADC + ∠BCD = 180°, because they are interior angles on the same side of the transversal. Since ∠ADC is given as 60°, ∠BCD = 120°. Similarly, we find ∠ABC = 60°.

content.text:
Worked example: A four-sided figure ABCD has AB parallel to CD and AD parallel to BC, and a line from A to C inside it. Angle DAC is 65° and angle ADC is 60°. Find angles DAB, CAB, BCD and ABC.
1. AB is parallel to CD and AD is a transversal, so angle ADC + angle DAB = 180°.
2. 60 + DAB = 180, so angle DAB = 180 − 60 = 120°.
3. Angle DAB = angle DAC + angle CAB, so 120 = 65 + CAB, and angle CAB = 120 − 65 = 55°.
4. AD is parallel to BC and CD is a transversal, so angle ADC + angle BCD = 180°, and angle BCD = 180 − 60 = 120°.
5. In the same way, angle ABC = 60°.
Answer: Angle DAB = 120°, angle CAB = 55°, angle BCD = 120°, angle ABC = 60°

concepts.concept_name: Figure it Out (angles), Q1

content.text:
Figure it Out (angles), Q1: Find the angles marked below. In every figure two or three lines are parallel and a transversal crosses them. (a) An angle of 48° and a are corresponding angles. (b) An angle of 52° and b are alternate angles. (c) An angle of 99° is shown, and c is its interior partner on the same side. (d) An angle of 81° is shown, and d is its interior partner on the same side. (e) Angles of 97°, 83° and 69° are shown, and e is the alternate angle of the 69°. (f) An angle of 132° is shown, and f is its interior partner on the same side. (g) Angles of 58° and 122° are shown on the right line, and g is the angle in the matching lower left corner at the left line, corresponding to the 122°. (h) Angles of 75° and 120° are shown, and h is the alternate angle of the 75°. (i) Between two slanted parallel lines, the angles 54°, 70° and 56° lie along one straight line, and i is the alternate angle of the 54° across the steep line. (j) Three parallel lines are crossed by a line, with angles of 27°, 97° and 124° shown; j is the vertically opposite angle of the corresponding angle of the 97°.
1. (a) Corresponding angles of parallel lines are equal, so a = 48.
2. (b) Alternate angles of parallel lines are equal, so b = 52.
3. (c) Interior angles on the same side add to 180, so c = 180 − 99 = 81.
4. (d) In the same way, d = 180 − 81 = 99.
5. (e) Alternate angles are equal, so e = 69. The 97° and 83° are not needed.
6. (f) Interior angles on the same side add to 180, so f = 180 − 132 = 48.
7. (g) The 122° and 58° form a linear pair, 122 + 58 = 180, and g corresponds to the 122°, so g = 122.
8. (h) Alternate angles are equal, so h = 75. The 120° is not needed.
9. (i) Alternate angles are equal, so i = 54. The 70° and 56° are not needed, but they fit with i on a straight line: 54 + 70 + 56 = 180.
10. (j) The corresponding angle of 97° is 97°, and its vertically opposite angle is 97°, so j = 97. The 27° and 124° are not needed.
Answer: a = 48°, b = 52°, c = 81°, d = 99°, e = 69°, f = 48°, g = 122°, h = 75°, i = 54°, j = 97°

concepts.concept_name: Figure it Out (angles), Q2

content.text:
Figure it Out (angles), Q2: Find the angle represented by a in each figure. (i) Two parallel lines with an angle of 42°; a is its interior partner on the same side; a separate angle of 100° is shown but not needed. (ii) Two parallel lines with an angle of 62°; a is the other angle of the linear pair of the corresponding angle of the 62°. (iii) An angle of 110° contains an angle of 35°; the rest of the 110° is the corresponding angle of the angle that makes a linear pair with a. (iv) An angle of 67° and a make a right angle between a transversal and a line perpendicular to the parallels.
1. (i) Interior angles on the same side add to 180, so a = 180 − 42 = 138. The 100° is not needed.
2. (ii) The corresponding angle of the 62° is 62°, and a is a linear pair of it, so a = 180 − 62 = 118.
3. (iii) The rest of the 110° is 110 − 35 = 75, which is the corresponding angle next to a on a straight line, so a = 180 − 75 = 105.
4. (iv) The 67° and a fill a right angle, so a = 90 − 67 = 23.
Answer: (i) 138°, (ii) 118°, (iii) 105°, (iv) 23°

concepts.concept_name: Figure it Out (angles), Q3

content.text:
Figure it Out (angles), Q3: In the figures, what angles do x and y stand for? (i) Two parallel lines and a transversal: a right angle is split into 65° and x, and y makes a linear pair with x. (ii) Two lines cross above a lower line; the lower line makes 78° with one of them and 53° with the other, and x is the angle between the two upper lines.
1. (i) x and 65° fill a right angle, so x = 90 − 65 = 25.
2. (i) y and x form a linear pair, so y = 180 − 25 = 155.
3. (ii) The two lines make angles of 78° and 53° with the lower line, so the angle between them is the difference: x = 78 − 53 = 25.
Answer: (i) x = 25°, y = 155°; (ii) x = 25°

concepts.concept_name: Figure it Out (angles), Q4

content.text:
Figure it Out (angles), Q4: Angle ABC is 45° and angle IKJ is 78°. The points D, E and G lie on a straight line, and the rays EH and EF go up from E on one side, in the order G, H, F, D. The sides of angle GEH are parallel to the sides of angle ABC, and the sides of angle FED are parallel to the sides of angle IKJ. Find angle GEH, angle HEF and angle FED.
1. Angle GEH is the corresponding angle of angle ABC, and then its vertically opposite angle, so angle GEH = 45°.
2. Angle FED corresponds to angle IKJ in the same way, so angle FED = 78°.
3. G, E and D lie on a straight line, so the three angles GEH, HEF and FED add to 180°.
4. Angle HEF = 180 − 45 − 78 = 57°.
Answer: Angle GEH = 45°, angle HEF = 57°, angle FED = 78°

concepts.concept_name: Figure it Out (angles), Q5

content.text:
Figure it Out (angles), Q5: AB is parallel to CD, and CD is parallel to EF. Also, EA is perpendicular to AB. The angle BEF is 55°. Here x is the angle at B between BE and the part of AB going down from B, and y is the angle that corresponds to x where BE crosses CD. Find the values of x and y.
1. AB and EF are parallel and BE is a transversal. The angle x at B and the angle BEF at E are interior angles on the same side, so they add to 180°.
2. x = 180 − 55 = 125.
3. y is the corresponding angle of x where BE crosses the parallel line CD, so y = 125.
4. The perpendicular EA is not needed for the values of x and y.
Answer: x = 125° and y = 125°

concepts.concept_name: Figure it Out (angles), Q6

content.text:
Figure it Out (angles), Q6: What is the measure of angle NOP? The lines LM and PQ are parallel. At M the angle between ML and MN is 40°, at N the angle between NM and NO is 96°, and at P the angle between PO and PQ is 52°. Hint: draw lines parallel to LM and PQ through the points N and O.
1. Draw a line through N and a line through O, both parallel to LM and PQ.
2. The line through N makes 40° with NM, an alternate angle of the 40° at M. The rest of the 96° at N is 96 − 40 = 56, between that line and NO.
3. The two new lines are parallel, so the angle at O between ON and the line through O is also 56°, an alternate angle. The angle between OP and that line is 52°, an alternate angle of the 52° at P.
4. Angle NOP is that 56° together with the 52°.
5. 56 + 52 = 108, so angle NOP = 108°.
Answer: Angle NOP = 108°

content.text:
Worked example: In a picture, two upright lines run through a burst of spokes, and they seem to bend outwards in the middle. How can we check whether they are parallel? What causes the illusion?
1. Lay a ruler along each line: it fits the whole line, so each line is straight.
2. Measure the gap between the two lines at the top, the middle and the bottom: it is the same each time, so the lines are parallel.
3. The spokes cut the lines at many different angles, and the eye misjudges the angles, so the lines seem to bend.
4. A measurement and a reason can overrule what the eye seems to see.
Answer: The lines are straight and parallel; the crossing spokes trick the eye about angles

concepts.concept_name: What we found about lines and angles

content.text:
Summary
When two lines intersect, they form four angles. The vertically opposite angles are equal and the linear pairs add up to 180°.
When two lines intersect and the angles formed are 90° (i.e., all four angles are equal), the lines are said to be perpendicular to each other.
When two lines never intersect on a plane, they are called parallel lines.
When a line t intersects another pair of lines, it is called a transversal and it forms 2 sets of 4 angles. Each of the 4 angles in the first set has a corresponding angle in the second set.
When a transversal intersects a pair of parallel lines, the corresponding angles are equal. When a transversal intersects a pair of lines and the corresponding angles are equal, then the pair of lines is parallel.
When a transversal intersects a pair of parallel lines, the alternate angles are equal.
The interior angles on the same side formed by a transversal intersecting a pair of parallel lines always add up to 180°.

content.text:
1. Our opening question is settled: two creases on a sheet meet if they lean towards each other, and stay apart for ever if they are parallel; a transversal with equal corresponding angles decides it.
2. One chain: linear pairs give vertically opposite angles; equal corresponding angles give parallel lines; corresponding plus vertically opposite give alternate angles; corresponding plus a linear pair give interior angles that add to 180°.
3. Still open for you: why do the illusions fool the eye?

learning_objectives.objective_text: Students restate the facts about intersecting, perpendicular and parallel lines and about the angles a transversal makes.

objectives.objective_text: Students state that two straight lines on a plane meet at one point only, that they make four angles, and that measured angles show a pattern.
Students find the other three angles at a crossing from one angle, using that a linear pair adds to 180 degrees.
Students prove, without using any measurement, that vertically opposite angles are equal, using two linear pairs.
Students list the linear pairs and the vertically opposite pairs at a crossing and find all four angles from one.
Students explain that a measured linear pair may miss 180 degrees through measurement error, and that an ideal line gives the exact value by reasoning.
Students find that four equal angles at a crossing are each 90 degrees, and name such lines perpendicular, whatever their tilt.
Students decide which value to trust, a measurement or a reasoned one, and find the angles at a perpendicular crossing.
Students describe pairs of segments using the words point, endpoint, midpoint, meet and intersect with angle measures, and judge whether two segments would meet if extended.
Students define parallel lines, name examples around them, and pick out the parallel pairs in a picture of segments.
Students sort pairs of lines into meeting, crossing and parallel, and say why a line on a table and a line on a board are not parallel.
Students describe the edges of a sheet, fold it in half horizontally, and count the parallel lines after each fold.
Students fold a perpendicular and a line parallel to a diagonal, and decide whether folded creases are parallel.
Students mark parallel lines with arrow marks, one kind of arrow for each set, and perpendicular lines with a square.
Students draw perpendicular and parallel lines on dot paper, mark parallel and perpendicular lines, and explain how they spotted them.
Students count the eight angles, find the four vertically opposite pairs, and explain why they cannot all be different.
Students name the corresponding angle of an angle in a transversal figure, using the same corner at the other crossing.
Students name the corresponding angles in a transversal figure and count the different measures a transversal can make.
Students draw a second line making the same angle with a transversal as the first and see that the two lines are parallel.
Students check that corresponding angles of a pair of parallel lines are equal, and find the other angles from one.
Students see that when two lines are not parallel, no transversal gives equal corresponding angles.
Students decide whether two lines are parallel by comparing a pair of corresponding angles, and find angles when the lines are parallel.
Students draw two parallel lines with a set square and a ruler, and justify them by the equal corresponding angles.
Students fold a line parallel to a crease through a given point, and explain why it is parallel.
Students draw a line parallel to a given line through a given point with a ruler and a set square, and explain the method.
Students find the alternate angle by going to the corresponding angle and then to the vertically opposite angle, and justify that alternate angles are equal.
Students find all the other angles at a transversal of parallel lines from one given angle.
Students decide whether two lines are parallel by comparing the corresponding angle found by reasoning with the given one.
Students chase the alternate angle through the corresponding and vertically opposite angles, and use it to find angles and test lines.
Students find an interior angle on the same side from a given one, and state and justify that the two add to 180 degrees.
Students use the same-side interior rule on two pairs of parallel sides to find the angles of a four-sided figure.
Students find unknown angles in figures of parallel lines using corresponding, alternate, vertically opposite and same-side interior angles, and linear pairs.
Students restate the facts about intersecting, perpendicular and parallel lines and about the angles a transversal makes.

video_coverage.book_item: Book item: Farhan draws two lines that cross and measures the four angles with a protractor, going round the point: a = 63°, b = 117°, c = 63° and d = 117°. What pattern do the four angles show?
Book item: Farhan draws two lines that cross and measures the four angles with a protractor, going round the point: a = 63°, b = 117°, c = 63° and d = 117°. What pattern do the four angles show?
Book item: Two lines cross. The angle a is 120°. Find b, c and d going round the point, without measuring.
Book item: Two lines cross and a = 35°. Use linear pairs to find b and d, then show that they are equal for any value of a.

Book item: Two lines l and m cross, and the four angles are named a, b, c and d going round the crossing, with a and b neighbours. List all the linear pairs and all the pairs of vertically opposite angles.
Book item: Imran measures a linear pair as 63° and 119°. Their sum is not 180°. Does that break the rule? What should the second angle be?
Book item: Two lines cross so that all four angles are equal. Find each angle, and say what the lines are called.

Book item: Five pairs of segments are drawn. FG and FH share the end F, with 115.3° between them. AB and CD cross at X, at about 60°, a little past the middle of each. IJ and LM cross at Y, at about 80°, close to the middle of both. Describe each pair in mathematical words.

Book item: Two more pairs are drawn: ST and UV lean towards each other by about 2.5° and look nearly side by side; OP and QR keep about the same gap along their whole length. Are ST and UV likely to meet if extended? Are OP and QR?

Book item: Nine segments a to i are drawn on a grid. a, h and i are upright. c and g are flat. d and f lean one way, each along the diagonal of a square. b and e lean the other way, also along the diagonal of a square. Which pairs of lines appear to be parallel?

Book item: A square sheet has two flat edges. Fold it horizontally in half again and again. Count the parallel lines, including the two edges, after one, two, three and four folds. What is the pattern?
Book item: Fold a square sheet along one diagonal. Describe a fold that makes a line parallel to this diagonal and say why it is parallel.

Book item: A square sheet is folded in the middle both ways, the edges are folded to the centre line, and then two opposite corners are folded onto a centre crease to make triangles. Pairs of creases a and p, b and q, c and r are marked. Are they parallel?
Book item: A drawing has two flat parallel lines, two slanting parallel lines, and one upright line that crosses a flat line at 90°. How are these marked?

Book item: Draw some lines perpendicular to the lines given on the dot paper. There are two grids, each 3 dots across and 4 dots up. In the left grid, one segment is flat, 2 steps long, and another leans with 2 steps across and 2 steps up. In the right grid, one segment has 2 steps across and 3 steps down, and another is upright, 2 steps long.

Book item: Five shapes are drawn on a dot grid. Each corner is given as (across, down) from the top left. Shape 1: (0,0), (2,2), (2,4), (3,5), (0,5). Shape 2: (6,1), (10,1), (8,3), (4,3). Shape 3: (5,4), (7,6), (7,8), (5,8), (3,6), (5,6). Shape 4: (0,7), (3,7), (0,10). Shape 5: (5,9), (8,9), (11,7), (11,11), (5,11). Mark the parallel lines with arrow marks (a single arrow, double arrow and so on) and the angle between perpendicular lines with a square. (a) How did you spot the perpendicular lines? (b) How did you spot the parallel lines?
Book item: On dot paper, draw different sets of parallel lines. The line segments can be of different lengths but should have dots as endpoints.

Book item: Using your sense of how parallel lines look, draw lines parallel to the line segments a to h on dot paper (13 dots by 13 dots). Taking steps across to the right and then up or down: a is 1 across, 1 down; b is 2 across, 2 down; c is 3 across, 3 up; d is 4 across, 4 up; e is 1 across, 3 down; f is 1 across, 6 down; g is 5 across, 2 up; h is 10 across, 3 down. (a) Did you find it challenging to draw some of them? (b) Which ones? (c) How did you do it?

Book item: Which line is parallel to line a, line b or line c? How do you decide this? Line a, line b and line c lean to the right. A steep line meets a at one end and b and c at its other end. The angles the steep line makes are about 30° with a, about 29° with c and about 33° with b.

Book item: A transversal t crosses lines l and m. The angles are numbered 1, 2, 3, 4 going round the crossing with l, and 5, 6, 7, 8 going round the crossing with m in the same way, so that 1 and 3, 2 and 4, 5 and 7, 6 and 8 are vertically opposite. Can all eight angles have different measures? Can the five angles 6, 5, 4, 3 and 2 be all different?

Book item: A transversal t crosses lines l and m. The angles are numbered 1, 2, 3, 4 going round the crossing with l, and 5, 6, 7, 8 going round the crossing with m in the same way, so that 1 and 3, 2 and 4, 5 and 7, 6 and 8 are vertically opposite. Can all eight angles have different measures? Can the five angles 6, 5, 4, 3 and 2 be all different?

Book item: A transversal t crosses lines l and m. The angles are numbered 1, 2, 3, 4 going round the crossing with l, and 5, 6, 7, 8 going round the crossing with m in the same way, so that 1 and 3, 2 and 4, 5 and 7, 6 and 8 are vertically opposite. Can all eight angles have different measures? Can the five angles 6, 5, 4, 3 and 2 be all different?
Book item: In the transversal figure, 1, 2, 3, 4 are at the crossing with l and 5, 6, 7, 8 at the crossing with m, with 1 and 5 in the same corner. Name the corresponding angle of each of 2, 3 and 4.
Book item: A line l and a transversal t meet at X, and the angle a between them is 60°. Describe how to draw a line m through a point Y on t that is parallel to l, and name the angles that are equal.
Book item: Lines l and m are parallel, with arrow marks, and t crosses both. The angle a at l is 65°, and b is its corresponding angle at m. Find b and the other three pairs of corresponding angles.

Book item: Two lines l and m lean 10° apart, so they are not parallel. A transversal t makes 30° with l, and m leans 10° more towards t than l does, so t makes 20° with m on the matching side. Can the two corresponding angles be made equal by turning t?
Book item: Draw a line l with a ruler. Slide a set square along l and draw two lines along its upright edge. Are the two lines parallel? Which angles prove it?
Book item: Place the long side of a 45° set square so that it makes 45° with l, and draw along it, then slide and draw again. Are the two lines parallel? How can you check?
Book item: A crease l and a point A are given. Fold a line m through A parallel to l, and say why it is parallel.
Book item: Can you draw a line parallel to l that goes through the point A? How will you do it with the tools from your geometry box? Describe your method.

Book item: Lines l and m are parallel and t is a transversal. The angles a, b, d, c are at the upper crossing (a top left, b top right, d bottom left, c bottom right), and e, f, h, g are in the same corners at the lower crossing. If f is 120°, find its alternate angle d.

Book item: Lines l and m are parallel and t is a transversal. The angles 1, 2, 3, 4 go round the crossing with l and 5, 6, 7, 8 round the crossing with m in the same corners, so 2 and 6 correspond, and 6 and 8 are vertically opposite, and 5 and 6 are a linear pair. If angle 6 is 135°, find the other angles.

Book item: Lines l and m are cut by a transversal t, with the angles a, b, d, c at the upper crossing and e, f, h, g in the same corners at the lower crossing. The angle a is 120° and the angle f is 70°. Are l and m parallel?

Book item: Lines l and m are parallel and t is a transversal. The angles 1, 2, 3, 4 go round the crossing with l and 5, 6, 7, 8 round the crossing with m in the same corners, with 2 and 6 corresponding and 2 and 3 a linear pair. If angle 3 is 50°, find angle 6, and say what relation angles 3 and 6 have.
Book item: A four-sided figure ABCD has AB parallel to CD and AD parallel to BC, and a line from A to C inside it. Angle DAC is 65° and angle ADC is 60°. Find angles DAB, CAB, BCD and ABC.

Book item: Find the angles marked below. In every figure two or three lines are parallel and a transversal crosses them. (a) An angle of 48° and a are corresponding angles. (b) An angle of 52° and b are alternate angles. (c) An angle of 99° is shown, and c is its interior partner on the same side. (d) An angle of 81° is shown, and d is its interior partner on the same side. (e) Angles of 97°, 83° and 69° are shown, and e is the alternate angle of the 69°. (f) An angle of 132° is shown, and f is its interior partner on the same side. (g) Angles of 58° and 122° are shown on the right line, and g is the angle in the matching lower left corner at the left line, corresponding to the 122°. (h) Angles of 75° and 120° are shown, and h is the alternate angle of the 75°. (i) Between two slanted parallel lines, the angles 54°, 70° and 56° lie along one straight line, and i is the alternate angle of the 54° across the steep line. (j) Three parallel lines are crossed by a line, with angles of 27°, 97° and 124° shown; j is the vertically opposite angle of the corresponding angle of the 97°.

Book item: Find the angle represented by a in each figure. (i) Two parallel lines with an angle of 42°; a is its interior partner on the same side; a separate angle of 100° is shown but not needed. (ii) Two parallel lines with an angle of 62°; a is the other angle of the linear pair of the corresponding angle of the 62°. (iii) An angle of 110° contains an angle of 35°; the rest of the 110° is the corresponding angle of the angle that makes a linear pair with a. (iv) An angle of 67° and a make a right angle between a transversal and a line perpendicular to the parallels.

Book item: In the figures, what angles do x and y stand for? (i) Two parallel lines and a transversal: a right angle is split into 65° and x, and y makes a linear pair with x. (ii) Two lines cross above a lower line; the lower line makes 78° with one of them and 53° with the other, and x is the angle between the two upper lines.

Book item: Angle ABC is 45° and angle IKJ is 78°. The points D, E and G lie on a straight line, and the rays EH and EF go up from E on one side, in the order G, H, F, D. The sides of angle GEH are parallel to the sides of angle ABC, and the sides of angle FED are parallel to the sides of angle IKJ. Find angle GEH, angle HEF and angle FED.

Book item: AB is parallel to CD, and CD is parallel to EF. Also, EA is perpendicular to AB. The angle BEF is 55°. Here x is the angle at B between BE and the part of AB going down from B, and y is the angle that corresponds to x where BE crosses CD. Find the values of x and y.

Book item: What is the measure of angle NOP? The lines LM and PQ are parallel. At M the angle between ML and MN is 40°, at N the angle between NM and NO is 96°, and at P the angle between PO and PQ is 52°. Hint: draw lines parallel to LM and PQ through the points N and O.
Book item: In a picture, two upright lines run through a burst of spokes, and they seem to bend outwards in the middle. How can we check whether they are parallel? What causes the illusion?
